Lab 02

Windows Device Setup & Provisioning

End-to-end new-hire workstation provisioning performed inside a Windows 10 VirtualBox lab environment. All tasks performed live with real screenshots.

Environment
Windows 10 / VirtualBox
Type
Device Provisioning
Tier
Tier 1 Support
Status
Completed
Date
May 2026
Windows 10 Oracle VirtualBox Device Manager User Accounts Windows Update 4 tasks completed

Goal

Simulate the end-to-end process of provisioning a Windows 10 workstation for a new employee. This lab documents the standard steps a Tier 1 helpdesk analyst would follow: creating a local user account with least-privilege permissions, auditing Windows Update status, inspecting Device Manager for driver errors, and documenting findings as a formal support record.

Task 01 — Create Local User Account

Situation

New employee needs a workstation account before their first day

A simulated onboarding request required creating a local Windows account for a new hire named Emily Ramirez with standard user permissions only, following the principle of least privilege.

Navigated to Settings → Accounts → Family & other users. Clicked "Add someone else to this PC", selected "I don't have this person's sign-in information", then "Add a user without a Microsoft account".

Settings → Accounts → Family & other users — starting point for new user creation

Created account with username EmilyRamirez and a temporary password. Verified the account appeared under Other users as a Local account.

EmilyRamirez successfully created as a Local account under Other users

Opened Computer Management → Local Users and Groups → Users to verify group membership.

Computer Management → Users — EmilyRamirez visible in the user list

EmilyRamirez Properties → Member Of — confirmed standard user permissions (Users group only)

Account created successfully with standard user permissions. Least-privilege principle confirmed via Computer Management.

Task 02 — Windows Update Audit

Situation

Workstation update status must be verified before new-hire handover

Update status was audited to confirm the machine was current or to document any outstanding issues before handing the device to the new employee.

Navigated to Settings → Update & Security → Windows Update. Clicked "Check for updates". Windows reported this version of Windows 10 has reached end of support.

Windows Update — device flagged as end-of-support. Security updates no longer available.

Windows Update actively scanning for available updates

Device running end-of-support Windows 10. No security updates available. Flagged for OS upgrade — escalated to Tier 2 / system administrator.

Task 03 — Device Manager Driver Audit

Situation

All hardware must be verified before device handover

A driver audit was performed using Device Manager to confirm all hardware was recognised and functioning correctly before the device was handed to the new employee.

Opened Device Manager. Identified Base System Device under Other devices with a yellow warning triangle — missing driver.

Device Manager — Base System Device visible under Other devices with warning icon

Base System Device — unrecognised hardware with no driver installed

Right-clicked Base System Device → Update driver → Search automatically for drivers.

Update Drivers dialog — automatic search selected as first resolution attempt

Driver update failed — Windows could not find driver automatically. Next step: manufacturer website.

Missing driver on Base System Device. Automatic update unsuccessful. Next step in physical environment: identify hardware ID, download driver from manufacturer support page. Documented for escalation.

Audited Device Manager — Base System Device missing driver, automatic update failed, documented for follow-up.
ResolutionUser account provisioned and verified. Update status documented. Driver issue logged for escalation.
Time to resolveApprox. 45 minutes
StatusPartially resolved — Escalation required for OS upgrade and driver

What I Learned

  • How to create a local Windows user account without a Microsoft account using Settings → Family & other users
  • How to verify standard user permissions using Computer Management → Local Users and Groups → Member Of
  • How to identify and document an end-of-support OS status and understand the escalation path
  • How to use Device Manager to audit hardware and identify devices with missing drivers
  • How to attempt an automatic driver update and document the outcome when it fails
  • The importance of documenting partial resolutions clearly so the next technician knows exactly what was done

How This Applies to Tier 1 Support

New device provisioning is a core Tier 1 responsibility. This lab demonstrates the complete provisioning workflow a Tier 1 analyst is expected to execute independently — from user account creation to hardware verification.

The driver audit and end-of-support findings also demonstrate knowing when to document and escalate rather than attempting a fix beyond your scope. Identifying the Base System Device issue and flagging the OS upgrade are examples of professional Tier 1 behaviour: resolve what you can, document everything, escalate what you can't.

Lab 03

Browser Scareware & Malicious Notification Removal

Real-world end-user security incident — identified and resolved fake antivirus scareware delivered through malicious Chrome browser notifications. All steps performed live on a physical Windows machine.

Environment
Windows 11 / Google Chrome
Type
Security Incident / Malware Removal
Tier
Tier 1 Support
Status
Resolved
Date
March 2025
Windows Security Google Chrome Scareware Removal Browser Security Notification Permissions Resolved — no malware found

Incident Summary

A user's machine began displaying repeated security alert popups in the bottom-right corner of the screen claiming McAfee license had expired, files were encrypted, and Trojans were detected. The alerts appeared to come from Windows but were actually being delivered through Google Chrome browser notifications by malicious third-party websites.

This is a classic scareware campaign — fake alerts designed to frighten users into clicking buttons that would install actual malware or steal payment information. The correct response is to never click the alerts and investigate the root cause.

Step 01 — Verify Actual System Security Status

Situation

Multiple alarming security alerts appearing — determine if real or fake

Before taking any action on the alerts, the first step was to check Windows Security directly to determine the actual security status of the machine, independent of what the popups claimed.

Opened Windows Security → Virus & threat protection. Reviewed current threat status, last scan results, and security intelligence update status.

Windows Security → Virus & threat protection — No current threats. Last scan: 0 threats found. Security intelligence up to date. Machine is clean.

Windows Defender confirmed no threats. Machine is not infected. The alerts are not coming from Windows — they are scareware delivered through the browser. Do not click any popup buttons.

Step 02 — Identify the Source of the Popups

Situation

Determine why fake security alerts are appearing

With the machine confirmed clean, the next step was to identify where the popups were actually coming from. Key indicator: the alerts showed suspicious website addresses like adjustnetwork.co.in in small text — a tell-tale sign of browser notification scareware.

Observed that popups were appearing as Chrome browser notifications, not Windows system alerts. The domain adjustnetwork.co.in was visible in multiple alerts — a known scareware distribution domain. Alerts included fake McAfee expiry warnings, ransomware claims, and Trojan detection notices.

Fake security alerts delivered via Chrome notifications from adjustnetwork.co.in — not genuine Windows alerts

Additional fake alerts including "Your PC is infected with 7 viruses" and "ALL YOUR FILES ARE ENCRYPTED" — all scareware

Root cause identified: malicious websites (adjustnetwork.co.in and jsgwegn22y7qwf.adjustnetwork.co.in) have been granted Chrome notification permissions and are using them to deliver fake security alerts.

Step 03 — Check and Remove Malicious Chrome Extensions

Situation

Investigate whether a malicious browser extension is involved

Malicious Chrome extensions can silently grant notification permissions to scam sites or redirect users to malicious pages. Audited all installed extensions for anything suspicious.

Navigated to chrome://extensions and reviewed all installed extensions. Found TeamSync Bookmarks flagged as unsafe, unpublished, and not trusted by Enhanced Safe Browsing. Removed it immediately as a precaution. Restarted Chrome — popups continued, confirming the extension was not the sole cause but its removal was still the correct action.

Unsafe extension (TeamSync Bookmarks) identified and removed. Extension removal alone did not stop the popups — root cause was notification permissions. Both issues required fixing.

Step 04 — Remove Malicious Notification Permissions

Situation

Revoke Chrome notification access granted to scam sites

The malicious sites had been granted Chrome notification permissions at some point — likely through a deceptive "Allow notifications to continue" prompt on a website. Revoking these permissions stops the popups at the source.

Navigated to chrome://settings/content/notifications. Under "Allowed to send notifications" found two malicious entries: cvlgn9ghubcc73921​9pg.adjustnetwork.co.in and jsgwegn22y7qwf.adjustnetwork.co.in. Removed both entries. Also noted mail.google.com was listed — left this intact as it is legitimate.

chrome://settings/content/notifications — malicious adjustnetwork.co.in domains found under Allowed notifications. Both removed.

Malicious notification permissions revoked. After removing both adjustnetwork.co.in entries and restarting Chrome, fake security alert popups stopped completely.

Step 05 — Clear Browser Data & Strengthen Security Settings

Situation

Remove residual site data and harden Chrome security

After removing the malicious permissions, leftover cookies and cached data from the scam sites were cleared to prevent any residual tracking or re-triggering. Chrome security settings were also reviewed and hardened.

Opened Chrome Settings → Privacy and security → Clear browsing data. Used Advanced tab, selected All time, cleared cookies and other site data plus cached images and files while leaving passwords and autofill intact. Then reviewed chrome://settings/security and confirmed Safe Browsing was set to Standard protection with Enhanced protection recommended as the stronger option.

chrome://settings/security — Safe Browsing set to Standard protection. Enhanced protection recommended for stronger defense.

Always use secure connections enabled — protects against insecure HTTP sites

Advanced security settings reviewed — password breach warnings active, managed browser DNS settings noted

Browser data cleared. Chrome security settings reviewed and documented. Enhanced Safe Browsing recommended to user as an upgrade from Standard protection.

Example Help Desk Ticket

FieldDetails
Ticket #SEC-0017
DateMarch 31, 2025
CategorySecurity / Malware / Browser Issue
PriorityHigh
Reported byEnd User — Personal Machine
IssueUser reports repeated security alert popups claiming McAfee license expired, files encrypted, and Trojans detected. User unsure if machine is infected.
Steps takenVerified Windows Defender — no threats found, machine clean. Identified alerts as Chrome browser notification scareware from adjustnetwork.co.in. Removed unsafe Chrome extension (TeamSync Bookmarks). Revoked malicious notification permissions in chrome://settings/content/notifications. Cleared cookies and cache. Reviewed and documented Chrome security settings. Recommended Enhanced Safe Browsing.
Root causeMalicious websites granted Chrome notification permissions, delivering fake security alerts via browser notifications to deceive user into clicking scam buttons.
ResolutionNotification permissions revoked. Extension removed. Cache cleared. Popups stopped. No actual malware found on system.
Time to resolveApprox. 30 minutes
StatusResolved — Closed

What I Learned

  • How to distinguish real Windows security alerts from fake browser notification scareware by checking the source domain and verifying directly in Windows Security
  • How to audit Chrome extensions at chrome://extensions and identify extensions flagged as unsafe or unpublished
  • How to locate and revoke malicious Chrome notification permissions at chrome://settings/content/notifications
  • How to clear browser cookies and cached data without removing saved passwords or autofill data
  • How to review Chrome Safe Browsing settings and explain the difference between Standard and Enhanced protection to an end user
  • The importance of checking the actual system security status first before acting on any alert — never assume a popup is telling the truth

How This Applies to Tier 1 Support

Scareware and fake browser notifications are one of the most common security complaints Tier 1 analysts receive. Users frequently mistake Chrome notification popups for real Windows alerts and panic, calling the help desk convinced their machine is infected. A Tier 1 analyst who can quickly identify scareware, verify actual system health, and resolve the issue without escalation saves significant time and prevents users from falling victim to the scam.

This incident also demonstrates a core Tier 1 skill: staying calm when a user is alarmed, methodically verifying the real situation rather than reacting to what the alerts claim, and walking the user through a complete resolution including preventive hardening steps.
